title: Proper morphisms descend along fpqc coverings
statement: Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme], and let $\{g_i:S_i\to S\}_{i\in I}$ be an fpqc covering [def-weil-pbc-fpqc-covering]. Write $f_i:X\times_SS_i\to S_i$ for the second projection of the fibre product [def-pc-fibre-product]. If every $f_i$ is proper [def-weil-proper-morphism], then $f$ is proper.

proof.text: For each $i$, properness of $f_i$ means that $f_i$ is separated, universally closed and of finite type. Finite type means locally of finite type and quasi-compact. Thus the hypotheses needed below hold for all $i$.
Apply [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-descend-universally-closed] to the given fpqc family and the universally closed $f_i$. It gives that $f$ is universally closed.
Apply [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-descend-locally-finite-type] to the same fpqc family and the locally finite type $f_i$. It gives that $f$ is locally of finite type.
By [lem-weil-pbc-universally-closed-quasi-compact], the universally closed $f$ of step 2 is quasi-compact. Together with step 3, this says that $f$ is of finite type by definition.

Put $D=X\times_S X$ and $\delta:X\to D$ equal to the diagonal. Pull the given fpqc family back along $D\to S$. By [lem-galois-fpqc-covering-base-change], the projections $D_i=D\times_S S_i\to D$ form an fpqc covering. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-over-pullback-diagonal-closed-immersion] to the $S$-morphism $f:X\to S$ and $S_i\to S$: it says exactly that the base change of $\delta$ along $S_i\to S$ is closed because $f_i$ is separated. As $X\times_D(D\times_S S_i)\cong X\times_S S_i$, this is also the base change of $\delta$ along $D_i\to D$. The identification follows from the fibre-product universal property: for a test scheme $Z$, both represent pairs $a:Z\to X$, $b:Z\to S_i$ with $f a=g_i b$. Under this identification the map to $D_i$ is $(\delta a,b)$ on both sides, so the isomorphism identifies the morphisms over $D_i$, not only their source schemes. Now [lem-pc-fpqc-descend-closed-immersion] applied to $\delta$ and the cover of $D$ shows that $\delta$ is a closed immersion. Thus $f$ is separated by definition.
Steps 2, 4 and 5 give universal closedness, finite type and separatedness of $f$, respectively. These are the three defining conditions for properness. Hence $f$ is proper.
